title: Tier-RAID for 3D DRAM tolerates weak lateral transistors
idea: Ideal: 3D DRAM where bad tiers do not matter. Closest: stack 36 tiers of which 4 are parity tiers, stripe each logical row across tiers under an erasure code, and let tiers whose lateral transistors show 100x worse leakage tails be declared erased between refreshes rather than refreshed faster.
why: Fact 2: relaxes the lateral-transistor specs that block 3D manufacturability and may pull 3D break-even earlier at ~11% overhead.

title: Deliberately weakened honeypot rows give early hammer warning
idea: Scale jump (cell -> datacenter security): each bank includes canary rows with intentionally narrowed isolation that flip after ~200 activations of their known neighbors. The controller scrubs canaries every refresh window, and a flip tells it to migrate victims and alert fleet security long before real rows (~1k) fail.
why: Lets designers drop costly per-row activation counters (area ~1-2%) while still catching hammer patterns early.

title: Buried n+ collector rails sweep hammer-injected electrons away
idea: Worse: let electrons emitted from an aggressor's repeatedly switching channel wander through the silicon into neighbor storage nodes. Flip: implant a phosphorus-doped collector rail (Si dopant only, no W fill) beneath the isolation between wordlines, biased to sink migrating minority electrons before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Fact 9: physically blocks the charge-migration part of row hammer, raising the flip threshold several-fold without metal shields or counters.

title: IBM Josephson memory density fixed with NbN kinetic-inductance persistent loops
idea: IBM's 1980s Josephson computer was cancelled largely because superconducting loop memory cells were microns wide and Pb-alloy junctions failed on thermal cycling. Fix: store bits as persistent supercurrent in ~100 nm NbN nanowire loops whose kinetic inductance replaces bulky geometric inductance, with cycling-robust Nb/AlOx junctions and moats that trap stray flux away from cells.
why: Persistent currents need zero refresh and dissipate nothing while holding; dense cryogenic main memory for superconducting or cryo-CMOS AI accelerators.

title: Fleet-wide weak-cell atlas predicts new dies' failures from lot genealogy
idea: Scale jump (one cell -> global fleet): aggregate ECC-corrected-error addresses from millions of deployed DIMMs, keyed by fab lot, wafer XY and die coordinate, into a Bayesian prior; a new die's likely weak rows are predicted from its genealogy and pre-mapped before boot. In-field profiling drops from hours to seconds and the prior catches rare tails that factory tests miss.
why: Retention/VRT tail coverage without long factory bakes; targets a ~5-10x reduction in uncorrected-error escapes and in test time per die.

title: Eliminate one-shot reads: NAND-style read-retry for nondestructive BEOL gain cells
idea: A low-temperature 2T/3T gain cell reads without destroying its charge. So when ECC fails, the controller re-reads at shifted reference levels from a per-region table learned from drift history until the codeword decodes, as NAND read-retry does.
why: Tolerates the wider threshold distributions of cheap <=400 C transistors at a tiny average latency penalty (retries are rare), relaxing device uniformity requirements several-fold.

title: Continuous stressed-read margin probing predicts failing cells
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: idle bank cycles run nonstop stressed reads with a shortened sensing delay and an offset reference, the DRAM analog of flash read-retry, so cells drifting toward failure are found and migrated weeks before they flip.
why: Turns idle time into predictive reliability: ~10x fewer uncorrectable events and less shipped margin, needing only a reference trim beyond existing circuits.

title: Soft-decision re-sense with shifted bitline references
idea: Ideal: never lose a bit, even when the cell signal is nearly zero. Closest: when the fast decoder fails, the row is re-sensed twice more with the bitline precharge shifted by +/-15 mV, producing per-bit confidence (like NAND read-retry) that feeds a soft-decision decoder able to recover cells with only ~20 mV of signal.
why: Facts 1 and 3: roughly doubles usable cell margin, enabling smaller capacitors or longer refresh at the price of rare slow reads.

title: Redundant-residue in-DRAM arithmetic self-corrects low-voltage compute errors
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: bit-serial compute sense amps | integration: processing-in-memory subarrays | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Values are stored as residues modulo small coprime moduli plus two redundant moduli; sense-amp adders do multiply-accumulate in each residue channel independently at 0.4 V, and the redundant residues locate and correct a faulty channel.
why: Constraint/Fact 5: data never leaves the subarray, ~10-20x less energy than moving it to an accelerator; residues confine errors so low-voltage compute stays exact.

title: Substitute mains power with betavoltaic trickle power for long-retention DRAM
idea: Pair long-retention cells (hours) with a power-gated self-refresh controller and an on-module Ni-63 betavoltaic source: refreshing 1 GB hourly at ~46 fJ/bit needs only ~0.1 uW, inside betavoltaic output, so contents survive outages for years.
why: Turns 'volatile' memory into effectively non-volatile with no new memory physics; the retention tail sets the energy budget.

title: In-array analog activation integrator replaces digital hammer counters
idea: Move hammer tracking from periphery into the array: each row gets one extra tiny cell that receives a fixed charge packet through a diode-connected path on every activation and slowly leaks; when its voltage crosses a threshold during the row's own sensing, a flag triggers refresh of both neighbors, with the leak rate setting the time window.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: per-row tracking for ~0.01-0.1% area instead of SRAM/CAM counters that cost several % of die and do not scale.

title: No ECC chip: exponent-only parity carved from mantissa LSBs
idea: Imposed limit: no x72 ECC devices allowed. For bf16/fp8 tensors, the controller reorders bits so the sign and exponent fields of 8 values share one SEC-DED codeword whose check bits are stored in the stolen mantissa LSB of each value. A mantissa flip causes a bounded relative error of under 1%; a catastrophic exponent flip is corrected.
why: Removes the 12.5% ECC device overhead (x72 to x64) and tolerates raw BER ~1e-6 cells, so cheaper or weaker DRAM is usable for AI weights and activations.

title: Solar MPPT perturb-and-observe tuning of per-bank refresh
idea: Solar inverters wiggle their operating point to track maximum power. Firmware in an open FPGA/CXL controller periodically lengthens one bank's refresh interval by a step and watches patrol-scrub correctable-error counts for a window. It keeps the step while errors stay flat and backs off when they rise, so it tracks each bank's true minimum refresh as temperature and aging drift.
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth 40-70% (fact 3) using only controller firmware, which fits a 24-month, $1M scope.

title: CRT rejuvenator revival: on-die microheaters anneal away retention traps
idea: 1950s TV-tube rejuvenators briefly overdrove the cathode heater to restore emission. Polysilicon microheaters under each bank let the controller move a bank's data out and pulse it to ~350 C for milliseconds against hydrogen-bearing passivation, re-passivating interface traps and dissolving the metal-related defects that create leaky tail cells, at power-up or in scheduled maintenance.
why: Water: contamination-induced leaky cells from lower-purity recycled rinse water and fewer clean steps are cured in the package, a path to ~10x less fresh water; also heals aging-related retention loss (fact 3); heater area ~1%.

title: Hourglass: lifetime-tagged tensors stored in refresh-free rows
idea: The compiler/runtime tags tensors whose lifetime is shorter than the profiled retention floor (activations, gradients alive <20 ms); the controller places them in banks with refresh suspended, and timed-out data is treated as expired rather than corrupted - the sand runs out only after the data is dead.
why: Fact 3: in training 30-60% of DRAM traffic is short-lived; those rows stop paying refresh energy and bandwidth.

title: Mayfly biologist: short-lived buffers tagged so they're never refreshed
idea: A mayfly lives a day and needs no long-term maintenance: the compiler or runtime tags buffers whose lifetime is shorter than the refresh window (ML activations, staging buffers, packet rings), and the controller sets a per-row no-refresh bit for them until they are freed.
why: Fact 3: in AI inference a large share of HBM holds transient data, so refresh energy and bandwidth for those rows go to ~0.

title: Diversity-pair cell: two capacitors with uncorrelated leakage physics
idea: Combine N-version design diversity with the cell: each bit is held by a silicon-access cell plus an oxide-semiconductor-access cell stacked above it, whose dominant leakage paths (junction GIDL vs. oxide trap-assisted) are uncorrelated; the pair is read as a charge sum, so a tail event in one device rarely coincides with one in the other.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): the product of two independent tail probabilities shrinks the refresh-limiting tail by orders of magnitude, enabling ~10x longer refresh; stacking offsets area.

title: Minify breakdown damage: self-clearing film capacitors burn off own faults
idea: Borrow the self-healing of metallized-film capacitors: build cell capacitors on a polymer-film or glass substrate with ~20 nm Al electrodes. A local dielectric breakdown vaporizes the electrode around the spot, isolating the short, so the cell loses ~1% of its capacitance instead of shorting its bitline.
why: Self-healing: dielectric breakdown, a leading hard-fail source, no longer kills rows, so thinner, higher-field dielectrics give more fF per area.

title: O: oxygen-vacancy recall pulses heal capacitor leakage drift
idea: During refresh-idle windows the array applies brief reverse-polarity, sub-breakdown bias across cell capacitors (plate and bitline swapped) that drifts oxygen vacancies back off the electrode interface, resetting the trap-assisted leakage that grows with time under bias.
why: Makes thinner, higher-k ZrO2/HfO2 stacks (more fF per pillar, fact 1) survive lifetime leakage creep; claim ~2x dielectric lifetime or ~15% more Cs at the same lifetime.

title: Skewed cross-bank row mapping scatters hammer victims across codewords
idea: Rearrange the address map so a logical row is built from physical rows at different indices in each of 8 banks (index = L XOR bank-hash); a hammered logical row disturbs a different logical victim in each bank, so any victim word gets errors in at most one 1/8 slice, which a per-slice symbol code corrects.
why: Row hammer: raises the effective uncorrectable-flip threshold ~8x with no counters; costs only address-hash logic.

title: Ladder-stop segmented vertical bitlines tolerate argon-free metal fill voids
idea: A dropped stitch runs the whole knit column unless loops lock; because argon-free fill (CVD/ALD in N2/H2 with no PVD liner) leaves more voids in tall vertical bitlines, split each vertical bitline into 8-tier segments joined by lockable switch transistors, so a void or open loses one segment, which is remapped to a spare.
why: Lets 3D DRAM tolerate the defect density of rare-gas-free metallisation (fact 2), limiting a single open to ~1/N of the string instead of the whole column.

title: Field-steered hydrogen re-passivates traps causing variable retention
idea: Effect: field- and heat-driven ion migration. For a mid-life self-heal, data is evacuated from a mat, built-in heater lines (wordlines driven in a heater mode) raise it to ~200 C for seconds, and a gate bias drifts mobile hydrogen from a SiN:H reservoir back to depassivated Si/SiO2 dangling bonds and GIDL-site traps that create variable-retention cells.
why: Retention-tail growth with age and hammer-induced interface damage: restores tails to near time-zero, so refresh intervals stay long and parts are healed instead of retired.

title: Substitute stored KV caches with NV lineage tokens and deterministic recompute
idea: Instead of persisting huge DRAM states (e.g., LLM KV caches), persist only the small inputs, seeds and checkpoints in NV, and regenerate the DRAM contents deterministically after power returns.
why: Persistence cost drops by 100-1000x per session since only the generator survives; uses existing DRAM.

title: Error-correcting pointers rescued from PCM to absorb DRAM hard faults
idea: Error-Correcting Pointers (ECP) were invented for PCM wear-out and died with it. Fix by moving them to DRAM: each 64B line gets 2-3 pointer-plus-replacement-bit entries in on-die spare cells, populated in the field when scrubbing finds a permanently failing bit, so SECDED stays reserved for soft errors.
why: Absorbs the growing hard-fault tail of shrinking capacitors and TSV-stressed HBM dies (fact 6), raising usable yield ~5-10% and extending field life.

title: Titanium-magnesium hydrogen getter shields zinc-oxide channels from drift
idea: Worse: let hydrogen from passivation films and packaging diffuse into ZnO-family channels, where it acts as a donor and shifts threshold. Flip: deposit a thin Ti/Mg getter layer (abundant, hydride-forming) above the oxide-semiconductor tier and inside the package seal so stray hydrogen is chemically captured before it reaches the channel.
why: Reliability of In/Ga-free oxide cells: removes a leading cause of Vt drift, keeping retention stable over life without scarce-element channel stabilizers.

title: Archaeologist's fragments: profiled weak bits decoded as erasures, doubling correction
idea: An archaeologist reconstructs a pot knowing which shards are missing: online profiling keeps a map of the weak cells (retention- and hammer-prone), and the decoder treats those positions as erasures; a distance-d code corrects d-1 erasures but only (d-1)/2 unknown errors.
why: With the same parity budget, about twice as many weak cells can be tolerated, so marginal dies are accepted and more cells pass test.

title: Half the voltage: 0.5 V array rescued by on-die BCH
idea: Imposed limit: half the array voltage. Run VARY at ~0.5 V with offset-cancelling sense amplifiers and accept raw BER ~1e-5 from the reduced sense margin. A low-latency on-die BCH(t=2) code per 128 bits, decoded in parallel with column select, cleans up the result.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: CV^2 array energy falls ~4x at ~6% check-bit overhead and ~1-2 ns decode latency.

title: Substitute UPS spend with NV-memory datacenters selling instant demand response
idea: Business model: datacenters with persistent working memory can drop to zero power within milliseconds and resume exactly, so they sell fast frequency/demand-response capacity to grid operators; the revenue subsidizes the NV memory premium.
why: Energy and capital: grid services revenue (~$50-150/kW-yr) can offset NV memory cost and shrink UPS/battery capex.

title: Andon-cord fleet telemetry loop from datacenters back to fab test
idea: At Toyota, any worker can pull the andon cord and push a root cause upstream. A neutral consortium collects anonymized per-die correctable-error signatures from hyperscaler fleets, keyed by die ID, and correlates them with wafer, lot and die position. It reports back to the fabs which test screens can relax and which must tighten. Data platform plus two pilots fit in $1M.
why: Test time down 20-30%, fewer good dies binned down, and fewer field DUEs. It also gives a U.S. entrant a feedback channel it could not otherwise get.

title: Paddlefish stochastic resonance: dithered multi-reads of non-destructive cheap cells
idea: Paddlefish electroreceptors use ambient noise to detect sub-threshold prey fields; for non-destructive-read cheap gain cells whose signal sits near the sense threshold, inject a known dither on the reference and take 8-16 rapid comparator samples, averaging to resolve signals ~5x below single-shot noise.
why: Lets the cheapest cells (tiny storage nodes, mature-node or printed transistors with wide Vt spread) be read reliably by spending ~8x read latency; enabler for ~100x cheaper stacked cheap tiers.

title: Grade-mixed ranks: Reed-Solomon makes one cheap die harmless
idea: Ideal: any die can be used. Closest: a rank uses symbol-level Reed-Solomon over 10 chips with 2 check chips, which lets one chip per rank be a cheap C-grade die with raw BER ~1e-5 (treated as a known-unreliable symbol) while the module still meets server RAS targets.
why: Supply and cost: absorbs down-binned dies into server modules, lowering module cost ~10-15%.

title: Substitute chipkill inside a DIMM with erasure coding across CXL devices
idea: Stripe memory across a pool of CXL memory devices with an RS(10,2)-style code so any whole device can fail; this allows cheap, lower-grade modules with no per-module ECC chips.
why: Cost per bit and supply: ~17% overhead buys whole-device fault tolerance, enabling commodity or downbinned DRAM in servers.

title: Core-stack parity plane revived: XOR row rebuilds any killed wordline
idea: Many core memories carried an extra parity plane computed across all bit planes. Each subarray gets one XOR parity row, kept up to date in a small per-subarray SRAM latch on every write and written back at refresh, so a whole wordline lost to a particle short, a hammer burst or a stuck driver is rebuilt from the other rows and remapped in the field.
why: Water: whole-wordline kills are the dominant yield loss from particles left by dry cleaning; rebuilding them lets an all-dry, ~10x-lower-water flow hold yield for ~0.2% extra rows plus latch area.

title: Resonant adiabatic wordline drivers recycle charge and soften hammer edges
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: standard | integration: monolithic + in-package LC tank inductor | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Wordlines are swung by a shared resonant LC tank with a ~2 ns sinusoidal ramp, returning most wordline charge to the tank instead of dumping it, and the slower dV/dt cuts capacitive coupling and electron injection into neighbour rows.
why: Constraint: wordline plus ~30%-efficient VPP-pump energy falls ~5-10x; Fact 9: smoother edges raise the hammer threshold modestly.

title: Catalyst regeneration: in-field thermal anneal heals aged DRAM
idea: Adapted from refineries that regenerate fouled catalyst with heat instead of replacing it: DIMMs carry a thin-film PCB heater and thermistor (board-level and trailing-node parts) and, during scheduled windows with data evacuated, bake their dies at ~150-175 C for about an hour to anneal interface traps and restore hydrogen passivation degraded by hot-carrier and hammer stress.
why: Retention tail and aging (facts 3, 9): trap generation drives variable retention and rising error rates; partial recovery could extend module life and keep refresh rates low, stretching the installed base without new wafers.

title: U: enrichment-cascade grading of secondhand DRAM for matched workloads
idea: Like centrifuge cascades enriching U-235, a line of FPGA testers in series progressively sorts used DIMMs by retention, hammer threshold and error history into grades, each sold with a workload certificate (error-tolerant AI cache, general compute, critical).
why: Recovers decommissioned modules into usable supply during the 4x price spike with minimal capital.

title: Navigator's dead reckoning: sense reference shifted by time-since-refresh
idea: A navigator estimates position from elapsed time and speed: the controller knows each row's time since last refresh and the temperature, and before sensing it shifts the bitline precharge or reference-cell level by the expected decay, so a sagging '1' still resolves correctly.
why: Fact 3: roughly doubles effective retention of tail cells, halving refresh at near-zero area cost.

title: Analog charge accumulator per row counts activations without SRAM
idea: Worse: track hammering with large SRAM counter tables in the periphery. Flip: give each row one extra MOS capacitor (pure Si) that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks slowly; when its voltage crosses a threshold the neighbors are refreshed and the accumulator resets.
why: Facts 7 and 9: per-row tracking at <0.5% area, no SRAM tables, silicon only.

title: Negative wordline undershoot sweeps hammer-injected electrons back
idea: Effect: minority-carrier drift and recombination. Part of row hammer is electrons injected from the aggressor's inverted channel diffusing to the victim storage node; right after precharge, the aggressor wordline gets a ~2 ns negative undershoot that accumulates holes under the gate and recombines or drifts the injected electron cloud back before it reaches the victim. Only the wordline driver waveform changes.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): could raise HCfirst from ~1k toward 5-10k activations, shrinking tracker tables and mitigation refreshes ~5x.

title: Never discard: modules shrink capacity gracefully as spares run out
idea: Rule: no module is ever thrown away for errors. Firmware consumes spare rows via soft PPR. When spares are exhausted, it offlines failing 2 MB regions and advertises reduced capacity through CXL dynamic capacity, and the OS migrates pages away. End-of-life modules are resold at their measured remaining capacity.
why: Extends module life ~2x and keeps ~95% of a module's bits in service instead of discarding 100% at the first uncorrectable error.

title: Pressure cooker: high-pressure deuterium anneal plus nitride reservoir hardens interfaces
idea: Cook wafers in ~20 atm D2 at ~400 C so access-transistor and storage-node interfaces are passivated with Si-D (several times more resistant to depassivation than Si-H), capped by a deuterium-rich SiN reservoir that re-passivates bonds broken during 10 years at 125 C.
why: Interface-trap growth drives retention-tail drift at high temperature; ~3-10x slower drift keeps refresh constant over life.

title: Odd and even buried wordlines at different depths
idea: Inverts 'all wordlines sit at the same depth': the single added mask covers even rows during an extra recess etch so odd buried wordlines sit ~15-20 nm deeper, staggering aggressor gates vertically away from neighbor storage-node junctions without changing pitch.
why: Weakens passing-gate and neighbor coupling, the dominant hammer paths at F~12 nm (fact 9); estimated 3-5x higher hammer threshold.

title: Cu: copper conductive-bridge antifuses give unlimited in-field row remapping
idea: Replace one-time fuses in the repair block with Cu-ion conductive-bridge cells programmable at ~1.5 V in the field, so the controller can remap hundreds of failing rows and columns over life (and undo them), instead of DDR5's handful of post-package-repair slots.
why: Self-healing repair makes weaker arrays acceptable: less test guardband, higher yield and fewer DIMM replacements.

title: Ice cube in drink: metal phase-change buffer clamps junction peaks
idea: A sealed pocket of low-melting alloy (Sn-Bi eutectic, ~138 C) in the package lid absorbs latent heat, so at 125 C ambient, self-heating bursts are capped near the melt point instead of spiking 15-25 C higher.
why: Arrhenius: removing excursions above 125 C roughly halves worst-case leakage and aging, so the part meets 10 years at 125 C without a 145 C guard-band.

title: Economist's congestion pricing: per-process activation budgets metered by controller
idea: An economist prices congestion instead of building more roads: the controller counts row activations per address-space ID in each 64 ms window and throttles any process that exceeds its activation budget, with the OS able to buy extra budget for legitimate streaming workloads.
why: Fact 9: dies with low hammer thresholds stay safe without per-row counters, and the costs fall on the offending process.

title: Exponent bits in strong rows, mantissa LSBs in weak rows
idea: Inverts 'all bits are equally important': rows are ranked by retention at test; the controller's address swizzle uses the fused ranking so sign/exponent bytes of BF16/FP8 words land in top-retention rows and low mantissa bits in the weakest rows, which are refreshed 4-8x less often.
why: The retention tail (fact 3) no longer sets the refresh rate for most bits; ~50-70% refresh energy cut with <0.1% accuracy loss on weights.

title: Row-buffer XOR tree: every activation doubles as full-row scrub
idea: Combine the activation path with patrol scrubbing: a hard-wired XOR tree under the sense-amp stripe computes parity over each 1 KB segment of the opened row and compares it with parity bits stored in that row, so every ordinary activate checks the whole 8 KB page rather than only the 64 B fetched. Mismatching segments are flagged to a background corrector before errors accumulate.
why: Retention tail and row hammer (facts 3, 9) and overfetch (fact 8): ~128x more bits checked per activate at no extra activation energy, so refresh can stretch 2-4x because weak-cell flips are caught early.

title: Chemostat refresh holds corrected-error population at a setpoint
idea: A chemostat holds a culture at steady density by tuning its dilution rate; let each bank's refresh interval float under closed-loop control that targets a fixed rate of ECC-corrected errors seen by patrol scrubbing, lengthening refresh until corrections appear and shortening it when errors or temperature rise.
why: Most cells retain for seconds; tracking actual behaviour instead of the worst case could cut refresh energy and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) by 50-80%, with ECC as the safety net.

title: Substitute symmetric ECC with Z-channel codes plus charge-minimizing inversion
idea: Since leakage only drains charged cells (one-way errors), use asymmetric-error-correcting codes that cost fewer parity bits, and store each word with a polarity flag that minimizes the number of charged cells.
why: Parity overhead and retention: ~30-40% less parity for the same correction and fewer at-risk cells, enabling longer refresh (fact 3).

title: Slew-limited wordlines reduce hammer coupling per activation
idea: Inverts 'faster wordline edges are always better': one mask adds a high-sheet-resistance poly resistor in each sub-wordline driver path, shaping a slower rise and fall that reduces the capacitive kick and hot-carrier injection each activation delivers to neighbors.
why: Hammer disturbance per ACT cut ~2-4x (fact 9) for ~1 ns of tRAS, with no counters.

title: Direct-tunneling germanium nanocrystal trap cell: volatile but wear-free
idea: Charge-trap flash wears out because FN/hot-carrier injection gives electrons enough energy to break oxide bonds. With a 1.5-2 nm tunnel layer, writes at <2 V happen by direct tunneling below the damage threshold. Discrete Ge nanocrystals mean one leaky path drains only one dot. Target ~1 s retention, >1e15 cycles, scrubbed like DRAM.
why: Capacitorless, low-voltage writes, ~15x rarer refresh. Endurance comes from energy-below-damage physics, not from margin.

title: Hot-carrier injection permanently nulls sense-amplifier offset
idea: Effect: hot-carrier injection and oxide charge trapping. At final test each bitline sense amplifier's offset is measured, and controlled high-drain-bias pulses on one transistor of the cross-coupled pair trap charge in its gate oxide, shifting its Vt to cancel the mismatch: a one-time analog trim with no extra transistors that cuts offset sigma from ~15 mV to ~3 mV.
why: Signal margin: the required cell signal scales with SA offset, so the same margin needs ~30-40% less Cs or tolerates more droop (longer retention); it also allows longer bitlines and fewer sense amps (periphery, fact 7).

title: Lifetime-tagged refresh-free banks for short-lived tensors
idea: A bit needs refresh only if it must outlive its charge. Compiler/runtime tags allocations with predicted lifetime, and activations, gradient buffers and per-step scratch (<20 ms) go to banks with refresh disabled. A per-region birth-time register faults any read past the retention deadline.
why: Refresh on AI parts: removes refresh from 30-60% of the footprint, and dies with weak retention become sellable as scratch tier.

title: Mycorrhizal parity pool: zero-ECC cheap modules share a common fungus
idea: Trees share nutrients through mycorrhizal networks; strip ECC chips and per-module repair from ultra-cheap memory modules and keep one shared erasure-parity pool on a CXL switch protecting hundreds of modules, rebuilding any module's failed lines on demand.
why: Amortizes protection (12.5-25% per module down to ~2-5% pool-wide) and tolerates high module failure rates, so the cheapest media classes become deployable; contributes to ~100x effective cost per GB.

title: Au: gold rows hold critical data in best-retention cells
idea: Boot-time firmware profiling ranks rows into gold, silver and bronze retention bins; the hypervisor maps kernel, page tables and model weights to gold rows at relaxed refresh and puts streaming and cache data in bronze rows with faster refresh.
why: Matches data criticality to cell quality instead of uniform worst-case refresh; ~30-50% refresh reduction (fact 3).

title: Core-stack strobe tuning revived: per-mat sense trims absorb CMP-free topography
idea: Core-memory stacks were tuned individually at the factory, with sense-strobe delay and threshold set per stack. At wafer test each DRAM mat is characterized and given its own sense-reference offset, sense-enable delay and wordline boost in a trim table, so a wafer planarized by dry etch-back and spin-on glass instead of CMP (leaving 15-20 nm topography and wider cell variation) still reads with full margin.
why: Water: CMP and post-CMP cleans are a large share of fab ultrapure water; dropping them along with wet cleans is the route to ~10x less water, and trims recover ~30-50 mV of lost margin for ~1 kb of trim storage per die.

title: Tailor's darning: aerosol-jet ink jumpers swap in spare memory chips
idea: A tailor darns a garment instead of throwing it away: modules are laid out with a spare DRAM footprint and open jumper pads; after burn-in, an aerosol-jet printer writes silver-nanoparticle traces that route the spare chip's lanes in place of a failing chip, followed by laser sintering and a conformal coat.
why: Raises module-level yield and lets marginal dies ship without BGA rework; an estimated 1-3% more supply from parts that would be scrapped.

title: Minify soft-error charge collection with thin films on insulating substrate
idea: Thin-film transistors on glass or sapphire have ~50 nm active layers over an insulator, so an alpha or neutron strike collects ~100x less charge than in bulk silicon junctions. Use low-alpha borosilicate glass so the substrate adds no emitters.
why: Soft-error rate falls ~10-100x, freeing the ECC budget for weak-cell tolerance instead of particle strikes.

title: Electron recapture pulse after aggressor activation bursts
idea: Reverse the hammer charge flow: after N activations of a row, the drivers apply a brief opposite-polarity pulse to the neighboring passing wordlines and local well contact to drift injected electrons back toward the aggressor's drain before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer: if electron migration is the dominant path, the flip threshold could rise 5-10x with no refresh bandwidth spent.

title: HBM base-die reroute layer swaps in a spare core die
idea: Inverts 'all stacked dies are essential': one redistribution mask on the base die adds a channel crossbar so a 9-high stack can map out any core die that fails after stacking and route its channels to the spare.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) drops toward ~5%; one RDL mask on a mature-node base die.

title: Sn: tin-bismuth microbumps self-reflow to heal opened HBM joints
idea: Use low-melting Sn-Bi (~139 C) microbumps with resistive heaters on the base die; when built-in self-test finds an open or high-resistance joint, the controller pulses local heat to re-melt and re-wet it, with spare TSV lanes as fallback.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) and field joint opens; recovering half the open-joint fallout adds ~10% usable HBM supply.

title: Micro-Czochralski seed dots grown with green solid-state lasers
idea: Copy crystal pulling at micron scale: etch seed holes in each 3D tier's oxide, deposit amorphous Si, and melt it with a 532 nm diode-pumped solid-state laser (not a XeCl excimer, which needs xenon and neon) so each grain grows from its own seed and every access transistor sits inside a single grain.
why: Grain boundaries drive the leakage tail of poly-Si tier transistors (facts 2, 3); location-controlled grains could let lateral 3D access transistors meet the <13 fA tail without rare-gas lasers.

title: Compress-then-protect: compression slack carries strong ECC
idea: Real 64 B lines have entropy well below 512 bits (zeros, pointers, small integers; 1.5-2x compressible with BDI/FPC). The controller compresses each line and fills the freed bits with BCH parity up to t=8. Incompressible lines fall back to normal SEC.
why: Retention/weak cells: strong correction for ~70% of lines at zero capacity cost, so refresh can relax ~4x.

title: Substitute NMOS access with PMOS access to blunt hammer charge injection
idea: Swap electron-carrier access transistors for hole-carrier (PMOS) ones in the array; holes have lower trap-assisted injection and weaker GIDL, so both the leakage tail and hammer-induced charge migration may shrink, at some cost in drive current.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and row hammer (fact 9): a speculative 3-10x hammer threshold gain and tighter retention tail if the hole-transport hypothesis holds.

title: Borrow image-sensor dark-current tricks: pinned STI sidewall implant
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: DRAM retention leakage and CMOS-image-sensor dark current are the same generation physics, so copy the sensor playbook: a p+ pinning implant along the STI sidewall keeps storage-node depletion off interface traps, plus a carbon-co-implanted gettering layer in domestically grown epi wafers.
why: Image sensors cut dark current 10-100x this way; even 3-5x lower tail leakage stretches refresh ~4x using U.S. wafer and process capability.

title: Substitute blind refresh with compiler-proven refresh-by-use schedules
idea: A compiler/runtime for AI training proves that every row of a tensor region is read or written within its retention time each iteration, and marks those regions refresh-exempt in a controller table.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3): for training memory that turns over every few ms, ~70-90% of refresh can be skipped.

title: Resonant-tunneling-diode latch makes the DRAM cell bistable
idea: Ideal: a capacitor cell that never needs refresh. Closest: a pair of series resonant tunneling diodes on each storage node forms a negative-differential-resistance bistable that holds the node at '0' or '1' against leakage with picoamp standby current, while the cell is still read and written through its single access transistor.
why: Fact 3: eliminates refresh entirely (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) if RTD peak-to-valley ratios can be made uniform across billions of cells.

title: Passivate last: high-pressure deuterium anneal after every plasma step
idea: Reverse the order and swap the passivant: instead of fluorine incorporation in gate and junction oxides, the finished wafer gets a final ~20 atm D2 anneal after all plasma and BEOL steps so no later damage undoes it, and Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier breakage far better than Si-H.
why: Interface-trap junction leakage and VRT tail cut ~2x, recovering fluorine's reliability benefit with no fluorine.

title: Poppelbaum stochastic counts store KV-cache LSBs in unrefreshed rows
idea: 1960s stochastic computers (Gaines, Poppelbaum) coded numbers as a count of 1s, so one flipped bit moves the value by one quantum instead of wrecking it. Each 8-bit KV-cache value keeps its 5 MSBs in normally refreshed rows and its 3 LSBs as a 7-cell count code in rows refreshed 10x less often; a decay flip there shifts the value by exactly 1 LSB, which attention tolerates.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): over half the cells of the fastest-growing AI tier skip ~90% of refresh at a bounded accuracy cost; density cost ~1.5x on those values, so it pays only for hot, short-lived tensors.

title: Deliberately weakened sentinel cell per row triggers refresh
idea: Box [medium: capacitor + 60%-size sentinel capacitor | access: planar | sense: sentinel comparator at high reference | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk Si | fab: DUV]. Each row carries one intentionally weak sentinel written '1' at every refresh; every activation and a low-energy idle sweep of only the sentinel column check it, and a decayed sentinel triggers that row's refresh, so each row is refreshed on its own physical clock.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: replaces worst-case 32/64 ms refresh with per-row physical timing; ~3-5x fewer refreshes, recovering much of the 10-20% bandwidth loss.

title: Latch resolution time becomes LDPC soft information for weak cells
idea: Effect: regenerative metastability, where a latch's resolution time grows as log(1/input). A time-to-digital tap shared across 8 sense amps records how fast each SA resolved, giving a per-bit confidence (LLR) to a soft-decision LDPC decoder over a 2 KB page, so raw BER ~1e-3 becomes acceptable versus ~1e-6 for SECDED.
why: 10x density: 1000x raw-BER tolerance lets ~0.5 fF thin-film Si cells stack 32 tiers at ~0.35x per-tier density (~11x bits/mm^2). Same cost: ~10% LDPC parity and decoders amortized across banks.

title: Substitute stochastic filaments with deterministic proton intercalation cells
idea: Swap filamentary ReRAM (random breakdown, high variability) for nanosecond protonic electrochemical cells where a gate pulse shuttles protons through a solid electrolyte (e.g., phosphosilicate glass) into a WO3 channel, giving smooth, repeatable non-volatile conductance states.
why: Error tolerance: much lower cycle-to-cycle variability cuts raw BER and ECC overhead; abundant elements avoid chokepoints.

title: Minify repair granularity to single 64-bit words via on-die CAM
idea: Replace part of the row/column fuse redundancy with a ~2k-entry content-addressable remap table per bank that redirects single failing 64-bit words to a spare word array. It is programmed at test and updated in the field.
why: Facts 4 and 7: a scattered single-cell defect no longer uses up a whole 8 KB spare row, raising 32 Gb die yield ~5-10% and tolerating tighter cells with more random defects.

title: HBM base-die SRAM patch cache retires failing rows at runtime
idea: Combine a CPU victim cache with post-package repair: a small CAM+SRAM in the HBM logic die intercepts addresses of rows that start failing in the field and serves them from SRAM, removing fused spare rows from each DRAM die and allowing unlimited, reversible repairs.
why: Self-healing and yield (facts 6, 7): moves redundancy from 8-16 DRAM dies into one logic die on cheaper logic area, extending stack life and accepting dies with more defects.

title: Uracil-glycosylase coding: make every charge-leak an illegal symbol
idea: DNA spots cytosine deamination because uracil does not belong in DNA; since DRAM retention errors are unidirectional (true-cells leak 1->0, anti-cells 0->1), store words in constant-weight/Berger-style codes polarized per cell orientation so every leak lowers the weight, becomes an illegal codeword, and is located by direction and fixed with a cheap asymmetric (Z-channel) decoder.
why: Retention tail (<=13 fA leakers) and refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% idle power): asymmetric codes correct leak errors with roughly half the check bits of symmetric BCH at equal strength, enabling ~4-8x longer refresh intervals.

title: CRT degaussing: trap-reset pulses to tame variable-retention cells
idea: Adapted from degaussing coils that reset magnetized CRT masks with a decaying field: using existing vendor test modes on current dies, the controller periodically applies a short decaying-amplitude negative wordline and plate bias sequence to idle subarrays, trying to drive variable-retention traps into their low-leakage state and hold them there.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): variable-retention cells force pessimistic refresh because they toggle unpredictably; if trap states can be biased, the worst-case tail could shrink ~2x, allowing longer refresh on parts already in the field.

title: HDR exposure bracketing: double sensing that flags erasures
idea: HDR photography brackets exposures to capture the marginal tones. A replica latch senses each line again with +delta and -delta reference offsets. Bits whose answers disagree are flagged as erasures, and the on-die RS/BCH decoder runs erasure decoding, which corrects about twice as many flagged symbols as unknown errors with the same parity.
why: Effective ECC strength roughly doubles, so the raw weak-cell rate can be 10-100x higher. That allows smaller capacitors or longer refresh (facts 1 and 3).

title: Boron-free, low-alpha die stack cuts soft errors at source
idea: Worse: keep borophosphosilicate glass and boron-doped films whose B-10 captures thermal neutrons and fires alpha particles into tiny cells. Flip: build the back-end with B-free dielectrics (P-doped or undoped SiO2, SiOC) and purified low-alpha Al and Si in packaging, so weak small-Cs cells meet soft-error targets without extra ECC.
why: Fact 1: smaller Cs raises soft-error sensitivity; removing B-10 neutron capture cuts SER several-fold, giving room to shrink Cs ~20%.

title: Desert cactus: Ga2O3 access transistors keep cells hydrated at 125 C
idea: The cactus's thick skin hoards water: a 4.8 eV bandgap Ga2O3 channel deposited by mist-CVD/ALD in BEOL forms the vertical access transistor over silicon-formed capacitors, where intrinsic generation at 125 C is negligible and off-current can stay <1e-20 A for 10 years.
why: Fact 3 at the 125 C/10-year constraint: retention stays at seconds instead of ~4-8 ms for silicon at 125 C, erasing the 8x hot-refresh penalty; goes beyond IGZO with a wider gap.

title: Spot-market auction allocating weak rows to error-tolerant buyers
idea: Markets price goods of different quality. The OS sorts profiled rows into reliability grades and runs an internal auction. Each process declares how much error it tolerates: kernel structures none, video frames, KV-cache and activations some. Weak rows that would otherwise be retired or refreshed 4x go to the tolerant bidders at relaxed refresh.
why: The retention tail stops setting the global refresh rate (fact 3) and becomes a priced resource. Refresh could fall 20-40%, and the ~1-3% of weak cells stay usable.

title: Magnify vertical link count: over-provisioned laser-drilled through-glass vias
idea: Stack thin glass memory layers using laser-drilled through-glass vias at ~4x the needed count, with any of four vias able to carry each signal through a switch. Open or high-resistance vias never kill a stack.
why: Fact 6: TSV-type yield loss (20-30% in HBM) shrinks to ~1%, and glass vias cost far less per hole than silicon TSVs.

title: Pharma accelerated-stability Arrhenius screening to shorten retention test
idea: Pharma predicts two-year shelf life from short accelerated aging. Short retention tests at three elevated temperatures, combined with Bayesian extrapolation of each die's retention tail and VRT probability, replace long nominal-temperature retention loops. The method is validated on 10k dies with a partner test house.
why: Test time and cost down 30-50%, and fewer false rejects raise yield. It is a methods and statistics project well within $1M.

title: Minify refresh 100x and decode known weak cells as erasures
idea: At final test, map each die's retention-tail cells at a 6.4 s refresh interval and ship the compressed weak-cell list in SPD. The controller refreshes 100x less often and feeds listed cells to an RS/BCH decoder as erasures, which corrects twice as many symbols as unknown errors; leftover VRT failures fall to residual ECC.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss cut by ~95%.

title: Magnify model tolerance: train networks on measured DRAM error maps
idea: Fine-tune networks with bit-flip injection that copies measured DRAM error maps: retention-tail positions, hammer patterns and true/anti-cell decay direction. Deployed weights then tolerate 1e-4 raw BER with no ECC and 10x longer refresh.
why: Fact 3: inference memory runs nearly refresh-free on cheaper bins and frees ~10% ECC capacity.

title: Bridge load-posting: measured per-module hammer limits written to SPD
idea: Bridges post weight limits from inspection rather than from design worst case. An open FPGA tester for commodity DDR5 (5 rigs at about $50k each) measures each module's minimum hammer threshold and retention tail in about 20 minutes and writes them to SPD vendor bytes. A BIOS patch then sets RFM/PRAC thresholds and refresh per module.
why: Most modules are far stronger than the worst case. Per-module settings cut mitigation bandwidth and refresh 30-60% (facts 3 and 9) with no new silicon.

title: Deliberately short capacitors, rescued by two-level ECC
idea: Inverts 'every cell must meet retention on its own': cut capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~45:1 (Cs ~3 fF), halving deep-etch and ALD time, and accept a fat retention tail handled by on-die BCH (t=2 per 256b) plus controller chipkill at a modestly faster refresh.
why: Sidesteps the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and capital (fact 4): ~15-25% lower array process cost and higher pillar yield for ~8% extra parity.

title: In-package deuterium reservoir re-passivates retention-tail traps in field
idea: Tail cells trace to single Si dangling-bond traps whose emission is exponential in field, and Si-D bonds resist depassivation ~10x better than Si-H. A Ti/Pd deuteride film in the package releases D2 during a 150 C self-anneal mode, which starts when the ECC-logged weak-cell count passes a threshold.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3), self-healing: holds the <=13 fA tail through the product's life and allows 2-4x longer refresh in later years.

title: Air-gap NEMS relay as zero-leakage gain-cell write switch
idea: The retention tail comes from access-device leakage, and a 10-20 nm gap electrostatic nano-relay has truly zero off-current. Use it only as the write switch of a gain cell, so reads never cycle it and contacts see ~1e10-1e12 cycles over life. The storage gate then holds for hours, limited only by gate tunneling.
why: Refresh (fact 3) essentially removed and the access-transistor tail eliminated, without a capacitor.

title: Atomically uniform hBN barrier collapses gain-cell retention tail
idea: Retention tails come from thickness and trap variation in amorphous oxides, where one extra trap opens a trap-assisted tunneling path. Isolate a 2D storage node (graphene/MoS2) with 5-layer hBN, whose thickness is quantized at 0.33 nm per layer and nearly trap-free, so every cell sees the same barrier.
why: Refresh is set by the median cell instead of a 1e-9 tail cell, for ~100x longer intervals, capacitorless.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrode isolates dielectric leakage hot spots
idea: Box [medium: capacitor with MnOx/VO2-type top electrode | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. The top electrode is a conductive oxide that converts to an insulating phase where local leakage current heats it (as MnO2 does in tantalum capacitors), so a weak dielectric spot clears itself during a forming pulse instead of becoming a retention-tail cell.
why: Facts 1/3: allows thinner, higher-k, more defective dielectrics (more Cs at lower aspect ratio) by healing defects; ~10x tail shift claimed.

title: Mg and Al oxide dipoles reshape gate edge to cut GIDL
idea: Worse: use W/TiN work-function metals and let gate-induced drain leakage set the retention tail. Flip: insert atomic-layer MgO and Al2O3 dipole interlayers only on the drain-facing upper part of the TiN/poly buried gate, locally shifting the effective work function to weaken the band-to-band field that drives GIDL.
why: Fact 3: GIDL dominates the <=13 fA tail; a 0.2-0.3 V local work-function shift could cut the tail ~10x and stretch retention, with only Mg, Al and O added.

title: 2050 engineer's self-healing: wordline Joule-heat anneals retention-tail traps
idea: A 2050 engineer treats defects as maintainable: in scheduled maintenance windows (data first migrated to a sister subarray), drive a controlled current through a subarray's tungsten/silicide wordline segments to Joule-heat it to ~300 C for microseconds, re-passivating the hydrogen-related interface traps that cause variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells.
why: Fact 3 leakage tail: heals the <=13 fA tail in the field, potentially doubling worst-case retention over life and reversing aging-induced tails.

title: Grocer's freshness label: printed time-temperature indicator predicts module aging
idea: Food labels change color with cumulative heat: a time-temperature-integrating indicator (enzymatic or diffusion-based ink, also readable electrically as a printed resistor) is printed on every DRAM module, and its integrated thermal dose predicts retention-tail and hammer-threshold degradation, so fleet software retires or re-bins modules before error rates rise.
why: Predictive retirement lets cells run on thinner margins safely and cuts DUE-driven outages, for less than a cent per module.

title: Pacemaker hibernation: stop refresh, decode the decay on wake
idea: Implants live on microwatts by sleeping. In deep sleep, turn refresh fully off for seconds to minutes and let the retention tail decay. On wake, a page-level BCH/LDPC code (6-8% overhead, sized for the expected tail at that sleep length and temperature) reconstructs every page before use, so no backing store is needed.
why: Refresh and self-refresh are 16-33% of idle power (fact 3). Zero-refresh sleep plus decode-on-wake removes most of it for phones, laptops and parked servers.

title: Z-RAM retention tail cancelled by differential twin floating bodies
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died when floating-body retention and disturb variability blew up at 45 nm and AMD walked away. Fix: store each bit as complementary hole charge in two adjacent floating bodies sharing a well and sense them differentially, so common-mode junction leakage and temperature-driven loss cancel and only mismatch decays.
why: Capacitor-free cell (attacks the charge wall, fact 1) with ~10x tighter retention tail at 2 transistors per bit, still smaller and simpler than 1T1C with a 70:1 pillar.

title: Kintsugi spares: repair rows built from a stronger cell technology
idea: Kintsugi mends pottery with gold so the repair is the strongest part; instead of spare rows from the same weak array, put repair capacity as SRAM or oxide gain-cell rows on the hybrid-bonded base die, so failed or weak rows remap to cells with no retention tail and no hammer sensitivity.
why: Frees the 2-5% of array area spent on in-array redundancy and gives repairs that never fail again, so more retention-tail rows can be retired (fact 3).

title: SIMOX-isolated access transistors remove junction leakage tail
idea: Ideal: a storage node with no leakage path to the substrate. Closest: build the cell array on 1990s SIMOX silicon-on-insulator so the storage-node junction sits on buried oxide, eliminating the substrate junction area and deep-level-defect generation current that create most retention tail cells.
why: Fact 3: junction-leakage tail cut perhaps ~10x, tightening retention spread so refresh runs 4-10x less often.

title: No Spruce Pine quartz: dirtier wafers paid for with ECC
idea: Imposed limit: no high-purity Spruce Pine crucibles. Grow CZ ingots in synthetic-silica or multiply reused crucibles and accept higher oxygen and metal content, which fattens the retention tail. Compensate with per-die retention fingerprinting, two-rate refresh and a stronger on-die RS code (16-bit symbols per 256 B), turning a purity spec into an ECC budget.
why: Relieves the >80% Spruce Pine chokepoint. A 10x fatter weak-cell tail costs roughly 3% extra capacity in check bits instead of a lost supply chain.

title: Deuterium-passivated cells with depot re-deuteration window
idea: Rule: the retention tail must be restorable at refurbishment. Interfaces are passivated with deuterium instead of hydrogen, using the stronger Si-D bond for slower trap generation. The package includes a gas-permeable window so depots can re-deuterate aged dies in a long, low-temperature D2 soak (~200 C).
why: Fact 3: a slower-growing, restorable leakage tail allows longer refresh intervals over the life of the part and more service lives.

title: Grid-cell residue codes: each modulus lives on a separate cheap die
idea: Entorhinal grid cells encode position with several periodic modules, a residue number system with built-in error correction; store integers and weights as residues modulo coprime moduli plus two redundant moduli, each residue on a different ultra-cheap low-yield die, so one or two dead dies are corrected and add/multiply run per residue near memory.
why: Lets 70-80% die yields and high raw error rates pass at system level with no known-good-die sort or repair, plus carry-free near-memory compute; a pathway to ~100x cheaper per GB.

title: Spin-Hall SOT-MRAM parity layer sits atop the array in BEOL
idea: Effect: spin Hall effect (spin-orbit torque switching). A SOT-MRAM layer built in the BEOL above the cell array holds per-row ECC parity and error-history logs; spin-Hall writes avoid tunnel-barrier stress (high endurance), and parity reads proceed in parallel with the DRAM read.
why: On-die ECC costs ~6-12.5% of array area: moving parity off the silicon frees it (~10% density) and makes stronger codes affordable for weaker cells; the non-volatile error log survives power loss for predictive sparing.

title: Dolby pre-emphasis writes overdrive leaky rows from recycled-water fabs
idea: Dolby noise reduction boosted quiet signals when recording and cut them on playback. Rows profiled as leaky are written with ~+150 mV boosted array voltage and a longer write time (pre-emphasis) and read with a matching reference shift (de-emphasis) from a row-class table, so cells with extra junction leakage still hold enough charge across a normal refresh interval.
why: Water: lets the fab run a ~90-95% closed rinse loop at 1-5 MOhm-cm instead of once-through 18 MOhm-cm ultrapure water (~10x less fresh water), whose trace metals widen the leakage tail (fact 3); pre-emphasis recovers ~2x retention on affected rows.

title: Magnify burn-in to days: catch variable-retention cells on panel racks
idea: Run every finished glass panel through a multi-day 125C burn-in in racks while repeatedly profiling retention. Variable-retention-time cells, whose telegraph states can take hours to appear, are caught and remapped before shipping.
why: Fact 3: VRT cells escape short tests and force refresh margin; catching nearly all of them lets refresh run 2-4x slower safely.

title: Airline fare classes: reliability-tiered cloud memory pricing
idea: Adapted from airline fare classes that sell the same seat at different prices with different guarantees: cloud providers offer VM memory in three tiers (full Chipkill ECC, single-error correction on relaxed refresh, detect-only on salvaged DRAM) at stepped prices, backed by separate physical pools and SLA terms stating error rates.
why: Supply and cost per bit: monetizes lower-reliability bits that would otherwise be scrapped and shifts tolerant workloads (batch analytics, caches, inference) off premium DRAM, stretching scarce supply.

title: Deinococcus polyploidy: scattered multi-copy for the critical 1% only
idea: Deinococcus radiodurans survives shattered chromosomes by keeping 4-10 genome copies and reassembling; replicate only page tables, kernel and allocator metadata 3-4x across banks with different physical neighbours and TSV columns, repairing by consensus on read, so the other 99% of memory runs with much lighter ECC.
why: ECC overhead and crash rate: crashes come mostly from corrupted metadata; strong protection of 1% lets bulk data drop from ~12.5% to ~3% check overhead.
